questions.question: How does error handling work in JavaScript — try/catch, error types, and async errors?
questions.title: Error Handling Js
questions.direct_answer: throw passes an error value up the call stack until a try/catch intercepts it; uncaught, it crashes (browser: unhandled error event; Node: process exit). Errors form a hierarchy: Error base → TypeError (wrong type operation), ReferenceError (undeclared read), SyntaxError (parse failure), RangeError, AggregateError (allSettled-style batches). finally always runs and doesn't swallow the return. Async: Promise rejections travel to .catch or await's try/catch; unhandled rejections are a separate event (unhandledrejection) — an async error NEVER hits a synchronous try/catch around the call that started it.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    T[throw e] --> U[unwinds stack: each frame checked]
    U --> C{try block in a frame?}
    C -->|yes| H[catch — handle by type]
    C -->|no — sync| W[window.onerror]
    C -->|no — async rejection| R[unhandledrejection]
    H --> F[finally always runs]
    A[await rejection] --> RETH[row into async frame — catchable ✓]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why async errors can't cross the sync boundary (the mechanism): a try/catch guards the synchronous frames of the call stack. When an async operation rejects, the original stack has LONG unwound — the rejection surfaces in the promise's own microtask context. await solves this by RE-THROWING the rejection into the async function's frame, making try/catch work across the async boundary — the specific ergonomics improvement async/await delivered over callback error-handling (where the first-arg-error convention had to be manually threaded through every callback).

finally's exact semantics (the corner cases): it runs after try's return VALUE is computed but before it's actually returned — verified: a return value survives finally. finally with its OWN return OVERRIDES try's return (the 'never return from finally' lint rule exists for this — it silently discards the original outcome, including swallowing errors). Errors thrown IN finally replace the in-flight error — the same hazard.

The anti-pattern catalog (what seniors name on sight): (1) catch(e) {} — empty catch, bug-swallowing; log at minimum, rethrow if unhandleable. (2) catch + console.log as 'handling' — it's reporting, not recovery; the user still sees broken UI. (3) try/catch around huge blocks — obscures WHICH line can throw and what invariants hold; wrap the specific operation. (4) Losing the stack — new Error('wrapped: ' + e) instead of { cause: e } (the ES2022 standard for error chaining that preserves the original stack for debuggers). The one-line summary: errors are values — pass them, type them, chain them; don't bury them.
